narrative.title: Why pharma, why now
narrative.body:
I spent the first part of my career in institutional finance, most recently at Goldman Sachs, managing a book of up to 20 multi-million-dollar corporate lending relationships. The real skill there wasn't the numbers. It was earning the trust of time-strapped people who had every other option available to them, reading what each one actually needed, and knowing dense, jargon-heavy contracts well enough to solve real problems with them. I held 100% retention across that book with zero escalations. In 2023, I stepped back for a planned break centered on family caregiving.

During that break I earned my national EMT licensure through UT Dallas, finishing in the top 5% of my cohort. Across emergency department and pre-hospital rotations I provided direct patient care to more than 150 patients, including trauma, respiratory distress, and other high-acuity cases, and completed coursework in pharmacology fundamentals. What stayed with me was how often a patient's outcome traced back to whether the right medication reached them, and whether the provider treating them had the right information at the right moment. That's the part of the chain a representative owns.

I know what I don't have: a sales title on my resume. What I do have is the underlying work that requirement screens for. As a full-time volunteer representative across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, I ran a three-state territory for 18 months against weekly performance goals, with a structured plan of action, daily pre-call planning, post-call evaluation, and disciplined CRM pipeline management. More than half of my new commitments came through referrals rather than cold outreach, because I invested in the community gatekeepers who could open doors a cold pitch never would. That is territory building, gatekeeper access, and rejection tolerance, learned in the field rather than in a classroom.

I also bring two things most candidates from a traditional B2B seat don't. I hold a clinical credential, so I can hold a real conversation with a physician and their care team on day one rather than spending six months learning how. And I'm bilingual in English and Spanish, which across DFW physician offices means real rapport with the front office staff and gatekeepers who decide whether you get five minutes or none.

I live in the DFW metro and I'm looking for a territory where I can bring analytical rigor and persistence. My approach is simple: know the product, know the territory, build real trust with the people in it, and keep working the angle until I find the right need and the right moment to close.

startStories.title: Territory Business Planning & Hitting the Number
startStories.teaser: Building the plan, then executing against it under real pressure.
startStories.body:
Across a three-state territory in Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, I worked a structured plan of action against weekly performance goals, and hit them for 12 consecutive weeks while onboarding and mentoring a new representative. Coverage wasn't improvised. It was planned, tracked, and evaluated.

At Vivint I sat on the other side of that number. I built the executive dashboards the COO and six department leaders used to monitor KPIs, quota attainment, and sales goal performance tied to sold volume and installation capacity, with findings presented in C-suite quarterly earnings calls. Understanding where a number should come from before anyone chases it is the analytical half of territory planning.

At Goldman Sachs, hitting the number was literal: approximately 20 complex lending transactions a week with exceptional accuracy and no room for error. That is the discipline of meeting hard output targets consistently, which is the same discipline a quota takes month after month.

startStories.title: Pre-Call Planning & Post-Call Evaluation
startStories.teaser: A call planning discipline built from scratch in a three-state territory.
startStories.body:
As a full-time volunteer representative, I built this process myself. Before every visit I set a specific pre-call objective. After every visit I ran a post-call evaluation, tracked through a CRM pipeline, capturing the objections and concerns I heard so I could handle them better the next time. That discipline is why more than half of my new commitments came through referrals rather than cold outreach.

At Goldman Sachs the same instinct showed up differently. When a client pushed back on a contract term, I found the misread myself, got internal leadership aligned, and resolved it before it became an escalation. Across the full account book I closed out inquiries on loan terms, interest rates, and payment structures with zero escalations. Prepare for the objection, then close with a clear next step, works the same whether the stakes are a contract or a prescribing decision.

startStories.title: Trusted Relationships & Developing Advocates
startStories.teaser: What I learned from the one gatekeeper everyone said not to bother with.
startStories.body:
Each area I worked had an influential community leader who was effectively the gateway to an entire network. Mine hadn't worked with a representative in years, and everyone before me said not to bother.

So instead of pushing him directly, I built a relationship with his wife first: weekly lunches, genuine friendship, listening for anything that told me who he actually was. She eventually mentioned he missed playing soccer with a group he'd lost touch with. I organized a recurring soccer event and told him all he had to do was show up. He did. Over time he went from ignoring us entirely to making referrals and mobilizing his own network, and eventually invited us to spend the Fourth of July with his family. Resistance is usually just information about what someone actually values. That's the motion this work takes: find the person whose voice already carries weight, develop them on their own terms, and let their credibility open doors a cold pitch never could.

At Goldman Sachs I held 100% retention across a key account book of up to 20 relationships with senior decision makers who had every option available to them and no obligation to stay. White-glove service, reading what each one needed and delivering it before they asked twice, is what kept them.

startStories.title: Respiratory Care & the Healthcare Delivery System
startStories.teaser: Learning the hierarchy from inside it, not from a training deck.
startStories.body:
Across emergency department and pre-hospital rotations I provided direct patient care to more than 150 patients, including trauma, respiratory distress, and other high-acuity cases. My clinical training covered airway and respiratory assessment and the pathophysiology of COPD and asthma, and I performed rapid-response airway support alongside an ER physician during an emergency tracheotomy.

I also supported care coordination with physicians and clinical nursing staff across patient handoffs and medication administration, and documented patient care records throughout. Understanding the physician hierarchy, the clinical nursing staff, and the workflow of a care setting is not something I'd need six months to learn. I've worked inside it.

That foundation extends to access. I understand prior authorization, reimbursement and coding, primary care referral pathways, and HIPAA obligations, which is the practical side of whether a therapy actually reaches the patient it was written for.

startStories.title: Market Intelligence & Business Analytics
startStories.teaser: Reading a territory with data, then sharing what you find.
startStories.body:
At 1-800 Contacts I built a nationwide brand marketing performance heat map across 41,000+ U.S. ZIP codes, enabling leadership to evaluate advertising spend against customer acquisition and regional market trends at the territory level. I also initiated an independent market analysis across all 50 states outside my assigned responsibilities, introducing a data visualization approach the team adopted, and trained the 10-person analytics team on the tools behind it.

At Vivint I analyzed operational and field performance data using SQL and business intelligence tools, learning both on the job well enough to deliver executive-level reporting within nine days of onboarding. I identified eight operational inefficiencies and uncovered a $2M revenue opportunity that informed executive resource allocation and business planning.

Reading local and regional trends, turning them into a plan, and feeding what you learn back to the wider team is the same loop a territory needs.

startStories.title: Compliance, Administration & Cross-Functional Collaboration
startStories.teaser: The unglamorous half of the job, done properly.
startStories.body:
At Goldman Sachs I interpreted 100 to 250+ page legal loan agreements to enable accurate billing, contract and regulatory compliance, and timely resolution of client inquiries, all while maintaining compliance with internal controls. Regulated environments, documented processes, and administrative work completed on time are not a burden I'd be adjusting to. They're the environment I came from.

As an EMT I worked under HIPAA obligations and clinical documentation standards, and as Executive Director of the BYU CASA chapter I drove certification completion across a 100+ advocate roster, increasing the share of active, fully certified advocates.

Collaboration shows up throughout: mentoring an intern and two team members at Goldman Sachs, onboarding a new representative in the field, training a 10-person analytics team, and coordinating with judges, attorneys, families, and community partners at CASA. Working across a matrix to deliver one consistent customer experience is a habit, not a new skill.
